newsitem.title: FRANCE: Nethold effect focus of Canal Plus results.
newsitem.headline: Nethold effect focus of Canal Plus results.

text.p: French pay television company Canal Plus is due to announce 1996 results next Wednesday and analysts will be looking for more information on the impact of its merger with Nethold this year and beyond.
Analysts said they expect Canal Plus to post a 1996 net attributable profit of around 700 million francs, compared with 666 million in 1995, a figure in line with the company's own projections.

Canal Plus is due to hold a meeting with analysts next Thursday morning on the results, and analysts say they will seek more information on how Canal Plus plans to restructure Nethold and how it will provision for it.

"The 1996 results have hardly any importance, but 1997 must see a result between zero and 50 million and, as the group promised, Nethold should not weigh down results by the end of 1998," said one analyst.
Canal Plus said last September following the annnouncement of its merger with Nethold it expected to break even in 1997, excluding exceptional items.
Another said he expected Nethold to bring Canal Plus 600 million francs of operating losses before restructuring charges for the months when the merger is effective this year.
"We will want to know Canal Plus's provisioning policy for possible restructuring at Nethold," said a fund manager.
Canal Plus's merger with the European interests of Dutch-South African group Nethold should take effect from mid-April.
Canal Plus has set a shareholder's meeting for March 28 to approve the merger and the nomination of three Nethold officials to the French company's board.
Nethold has operating losses of 140 million dollars and hopes to become profitable from 1999.
"The group has to become more international. It can do so with Nethold, which is highly complementary, but which has delicate health," said one analyst.
"In this context, either you believe Canal Plus is creating value or you don't," said another.

This analyst said that Canal Plus chairman Pierre Lescure has become the top man for broadcasting for Havas, which is to become Canal Plus's leading shareholder once the Havas/Generale des Eaux accord goes through.
"Lescure should have more freedom of action than ever, at least that is what one hopes," the analyst said.
A fund manager said Canal Plus currently has several problem areas. These include Spain, which Canal Plus has operated directly up to now, Italy and Nethold's territory in Scandinavia, he said.
"Canal needs to get to grips with the problem of a slowdown in the rate of signing up new subscribers, in France and abroad," he said.

Analysts said Canal Plus's difficulties in Spain could be alleviated if, as some published reports have said, Telefonica and Televisa, which operate a rival digital satellite group backed by the Spanish government, take a 35 percent stake in CanalSatelite Digital, Canal Plus's Spanish satellite unit.
Under such a deal Canal Plus, whose stake in CanalSatelite Digital is held indirectly via Sogecable, would reduce its stake in its Spanish satellite unit.
A Canal Plus spokeswoman confirmed that the company was talking with the Spanish government, but gave no other details.
